lessons.title: يا (yā) — calling somebody
lessons.gloss: O — the vocative particle Arabic puts before every name it calls, and two letters that stand between the reader and addressing anybody

segments.text: Chapter two taught you to give your name and to ask for somebody else's. Forty chapters later you still cannot call them by it.

segments.instruction: the time joiner from the lesson before — ḥīnamā
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the time joiner from the lesson before — *ḥīnamā*]

segments.text: يا حسن — yā Ḥasan — Hasan! (calling him).
يا جار — yā jār — neighbour!

Arabic does not address a person with a bare name. حسن on its own is a statement about Hasan; يا (yā) حسن is speaking to him. The particle is not optional politeness — it is how the language marks the difference between naming somebody and calling them.
Two letters, both long since yours, and no ending changes on the name.

يا (yā) is pan-Semitic and English has no particle of its own to match it. The one place English reaches for something similar is old translation — O Lord, O Israel — where the O is standing in for exactly this. It sounds archaic in English and is entirely everyday in Arabic.
It goes before a title or a kin term as readily as before a name: يا ابن, يا بنت, yā ṣadīqī.

segments.instruction: yā Ḥasan
yā jār … yā ṣadīqī
the name alone, then called — Ḥasan … yā Ḥasan
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the name alone, then called — *Ḥasan* … *yā Ḥasan*]

segments.text: What is the difference between حسن and يا (yā) حسن? (One names him; the other calls him.) Does the name change shape after it? (No.) And what does English use where Arabic uses يا (yā)? (Nothing, ordinarily — only O in old translation.)
Source: Unicode Arabic chart.

lessons.title: كرّر من فضلك (karrir min faḍlik) — say it again, please
lessons.gloss: say it again, please — the second half of a repair kit whose first half arrived four chapters ago, and the first command this book has ever given

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Chapter thirty-seven gave you the first thing a lost learner says. Saying it only helps if you can also ask for the sentence back.

segments.instruction: the particle from the lesson before, and what it turns a name into — yā
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the particle from the lesson before, and what it turns a name into — *yā*]

segments.text: كرّر — karrir — repeat.
كرّر من فضلك — karrir min faḍlik — say it again, please.

The please is not new: chapter six taught it. What is new is the verb, and the shape it comes in — this is the first command in the book, and Arabic builds one by stripping the present tense back to its bare stem.

Look at the shadda. كرّر doubles its middle letter, which is the same Form II shape as fakkara in chapter thirty-two — a pattern that means do it thoroughly, do it repeatedly. On the root ك-ر-ر, "to return", that gives exactly do it again.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the repair kit, whole

utterances: when: you did not follow. say: lā afham.
when: you want it again. say: karrir min faḍlik.
when: you are grateful for it. say: shukran.

segments.text: The inventory that measured this track said the repair kit was strong with one hole in it: sorry, excuse me, pardon, please and thank you were all taught, and I do not understand and say it again were not. Those two are what chapters thirty-seven and forty-one add, and between them they needed one new verb.

segments.instruction: karrir
karrir min faḍlik
the whole kit in order — lā afham … karrir min faḍlik … shukran
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the whole kit in order — *lā afham … karrir min faḍlik … shukran*]

segments.instruction: and get their attention first — yā Ḥasan, karrir min faḍlik
segments.source: [YOU SAY: and get their attention first — *yā Ḥasan, karrir min faḍlik*]

segments.text: Which chapter taught the please in this sentence? (Six.) Which earlier verb wears the same doubled shape? (fakkara, chapter thirty-two.) And what does that shape add to a root? (Doing it thoroughly, or again.)
Source: Unicode Arabic chart.

blocks.title: Guided Practice: the distant band — the first meeting, and what to do when it goes wrong

segments.text: The exchange this book opened with was taught more than a hundred lessons ago and has not been asked for since. It is also the exact place a beginner loses the thread. Run it cold, and put the new chapter inside it.

segments.instruction: the greeting and its reply, and hear the و at the front of the reply — as-salāmu ʿalaykum … wa-ʿalaykum as-salām
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the greeting and its reply, and hear the **و** at the front of the reply — *as-salāmu ʿalaykum* … *wa-ʿalaykum as-salām*]

segments.text: Five chapters ago this book could not say a verb in the present, deny a nominal sentence, join two nouns, ask a yes-or-no question, give a reason, or say that it had not understood. Say the sentence that was one tense away for thirty-one chapters. (lā afham.) Say what you ask next. (karrir min faḍlik.) And say how you get somebody's attention first. (yā plus their name.)
